03:15 < antagonizt> it's in
03:15 < Filip> ok
03:16 < antagonizt> i forgot a couple scan-codes... i'm updating now
03:17 < Filip> in the field, when doing a lot of simple input  this could be much faster than using a stylus
03:17 < antagonizt> i have tab, enter, ctrl-c, backspace... what else is commonly used that should be a two key combo?
03:17 < antagonizt> two or one rather
03:17 < Filip> i'll check some more for the interrupts, but it looks like the ones used in CE are all 'virtual' interrutps, ie just numbers used by CE and not  related to the hardware interupts
03:18 < Filip> it's some kind of abstraction layer between various different hardware solutions and a single codebase
03:18 < Filip> like serial is always irq 4 to the driver/application, no matter what hardware is underneath
03:19 < antagonizt> weird.. the serial CE code led me to believe the serial interrupt was 19 wich the vr4122 header says is a software interrupt...
03:20 < Filip> were exactly did you get that number ?
03:20 < antagonizt> the RE CE c code
03:21 < Filip> only during the initialsiation of the low-level drivr the real hardware interrupt is used exactly once: to add it to the mapping table. all the other code uses the virtual interrupt
03:21 < antagonizt> odd
03:21 < Filip> MapIrq2SysIntr
03:21 < antagonizt> do you think the companion has its own ICU?
03:21 < Filip> is the function used to map a real IRQ to a CE System interrupt
03:22 < Filip> with my knowledge of IRQ's I think it must be chained to the main cpu if it has it's own
03:22 < Filip> g_Intr2SysintrMap[Irq]
03:22 < Filip> g_Sysintr2IntrMap[SysIntr]
03:23 < antagonizt> could you write a fake CE driver that translates IRQs then?
03:25 < Filip> If I could find out where those arrays are ..... they live in the core kernel, for which there is no lib file.
03:25 < Filip> and public API's provide only one-way mapping: you can add to it, but not read from it :-(
03:26 < Filip> and even them I'm not sure it will hlep a lot: as I understand, there will be one 'master' interrupt for the companion, which is connected to the cpu
03:27 < Filip> when you get an interrupt from it, the interrupt handler will need to check with the companion what function raised the interrupt
03:27 < Filip> I'm thinking of creating some very basic test program (not even a full kernel) doing the following:
03:27 < Filip> clear all interupt vecotrs 
03:28 < Filip> (no serial code, since it also uses interrupts)
03:28 < Filip> use some kind of simple' framebuffer output
03:28 < Filip> watch the interrupts on the cpu while pressing buttons, touchscreen, insert/remove CF, connect/disconnect serial cable
03:29 < Filip> I expect all of these to trigger the same interrupt
03:29 < Filip> and then there probably is a mask somewhere on the companion telling what function triggered the interrupt
03:29 < antagonizt> yeah... it looks like jun sun updated his mips porting how-to... there is now some info on interrupts
03:29 < Filip> so you can dispatch to the correct  driver
03:30 < Filip> does this make sense ?
03:30 < antagonizt> we will need to cascade the interrupts, right?
03:30 < antagonizt> yeah... not that i'm an expert
03:32 < Filip> still learning on mips/irq's as well .....
03:33 < Filip> reading jun sun's
03:34 < Filip> hmm 'is typically an assembly code '
03:34 < Filip> think c code will do as well to start with, no ? once it's working we can optimise it
03:39 < Filip> since it looks like our 'super companion' chip is handling all/most of the i/o , we'll probably have only one external irq source
03:40 < Filip> going to re-read the cpu's manual (or at least the chapters about interupts)
03:41 < antagonizt> have fun... like reading a lawbook :)
03:42 < Filip> wll, i start to understand better how those interrupts are working, so I hope that part of the manual now makes more sense to me than it did whe, I first read it
03:43 < Filip> where you actually able to do a 'ls /' or something like that with your input driver ?

03:43 < antagonizt> did all kinds of things with it
03:43 < Filip> great, so it looks like kernel is pretty stable

11:16 < jal0> dont think so, due to the way the ASIC is created, each module would have its own irq, besides almost all the GPIO lines can be configured as interrupt sources.
11:17 < Filip> ok, I see; so I need to make a test progie to configure all cpio's ar interrupt source, and then just loop 
11:17 < Filip> cpio=gpio
11:17 < Filip> ar=as

11:18 < Filip> create a dummy interrupt handler that just prints the source (or a colored block on the screen) when an interrupt is raised

11:18 < Filip> just a really simple test proggie like the serial ones, eventually making different colored blocks on the screen for each interrupt
11:18 < jal0> planned on writing a bit of code that did nothing but return the status of the GIUINTSTATH and GIUINTSTATL registers
11:19 < jal0> those would show the stat of the GPIO interrupts
11:20 < Filip> well, if you're right about the ASIC using different irq sources for each device it would even be better for writing  the interupt code: no chained interrupts
11:21 < jal0> well actually there is a sort of chaining, have you looked at the ICU chaper in the vr4131 manual?
11:21 < Filip> not yet, planned on doing dso tonight
11:22 < jal0> ICU core only recieved interrupt signals from irq[3:0] (level 2) signals.
11:23 < jal0> we will still have to query the external device to determine the source of the interrupt
11:23 < Filip> does this mean you know you got an interrupt from GPIO, but no way  to tell which one ?
11:23 < jal0> as far as the cpu is conserned, each module of the ASIC is seen as an independent chip
11:24 < jal0> have to do some experimenting to determine the soure of each GPIO interrupt
11:24 < jal0> that or RE some CE code
